papers.title: CABrain: A Correlation-Aware Brain Foundation Model for EEG Decoding
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models have emerged as promising paradigms for decoding brain activity through large-scale self-supervised pretraining. Notably, most existing approaches employ masked patch reconstruction, in which randomly selected EEG patches are masked and recovered by the network. However, purely random masking may limit representation learning as informative patches from highly correlated channels often remain unmasked, causing the network to underutilize weakly correlated channels or serial dependencies. Furthermore, because these models are typically based on transformer architectures, their performance is influenced by the choice of positional encoding. Although positional encoding has been extensively explored in natural language processing and computer vision, few studies have adapted it to the unique characteristics of EEG signals. To address these limitations, this study introduces a conditional positional encoding method based on graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to explicitly model inter-channel correlations, along with an adaptive masking strategy that enhances representation learning by modulating the difficulty of masked patch reconstruction. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate graph-based representations into conditional positional encoding and introduce adaptive masking within EEG foundation model pretraining. Experimental results on ten benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed GCN-based positional encoding and adaptive masking strategies, both individually and in combination, achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance, highlighting their effectiveness in EEG foundation modeling.

Across ten benchmark datasets, these components individually and jointly achieved state-of-the-art or competitive EEG decoding performance.

papers.title: Chronic neuropeptide S treatment improves sleep architecture and reduces Aβ-related pathology in APP/PS1 mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances frequently occur in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although neuropeptide S (NPS) promotes wakefulness through the widely expressed NPS receptor (NPSR), its role in AD-related sleep dysregulation is unclear. To investigate the effects of chronic NPS administration on AD-related sleep disturbances beyond its acute wake-promoting effects. NPSR expression was examined in the hypothalamus and hippocampus of APPswe/PS1dE9 (APP/PS1) mice, a double-transgenic mouse model of AD. Mice received intracerebroventricular NPS (1 nmol/day) for 14 days. Sleep-wake states were classified as wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Sleep architecture and amyloid-β (Aβ)-related pathology were assessed in mice. Cell-associated Aβ levels, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation, and autophagy-related proteins were examined in BV2 cells. Sleep responses to subsequent intracerebroventricular Aβ₁-₄₂ administration were examined in NPS-treated APP/PS1 mice. APP/PS1 mice had lower NPSR protein levels in the hypothalamus and hippocampus than wild-type (WT) controls. Compared with saline-treated APP/PS1 mice, NPS-treated mice showed increased NREM sleep, reduced wakefulness, and lower Aβ-related pathology. Changes in sleep amounts were most evident during the light phase. Subsequent Aβ₁-₄₂ administration increased wakefulness and reduced NREM sleep mainly during the dark phase. It also shortened NREM episodes during the light phase. In BV2 cells, NPS altered cell-associated Aβ levels and increased ERK phosphorylation. NPS treatment was also associated with higher LC3B-II and lower p62 levels. SCH772984 attenuated the NPS-associated changes in autophagy-related proteins and cell-associated Aβ. Chronic NPS administration improved sleep architecture and reduced Aβ-related pathology in APP/PS1 mice. The BV2 findings suggest possible involvement of ERK signaling and autophagy-related processes in cellular Aβ handling.

papers.title: Automated intracranial spike analysis across sleep-wake states localizes the seizure onset zone in drug-resistant epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) are an established biomarker of epilepsy, but their utility for seizure-onset zone (SOZ) localization has been limited by reliance on short recording samples, research-grade detectors, and a primary focus on spike frequency. We assessed multi-day intracranial IED activity across sleep-wake states and its ability to localize the SOZ in adults and children. We analyzed simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG data from 17 patients in the EPILEPSIAE database (predominantly adult) and 10 pediatric patients at the Alberta Children's Hospital (ACH), with 48 to 72 h of data per patient. FDA-cleared clinical software (Persyst P15a) performed automated sleep staging and IED detection. We introduced a novel IED activity metric reflecting IED amplitude and the relative consistency of channel participation across detected events and used logistic regression with leave-one-patient-out cross-validation to predict SOZ channels for each sleep-wake state. IED activity was significantly higher in SOZ than in non-SOZ channels across every sleep-wake state in both cohorts. N2 sleep yielded the highest AUROC for SOZ localization (0.69 EPILEPSIAE; 0.77 ACH), but differences across states were not statistically significant. The presence of clinical seizures during the recording did not significantly affect localization performance. Automated intracranial IED analysis localizes the SOZ in adults and children, with only modest variation across sleep-wake states. Amplitude-aware IED analysis using clinically deployed software is a practical adjunct to presurgical SOZ localization. The modest effect of sleep-wake states suggests that clinical value can be obtained without state-specific analysis. This approach may strengthen presurgical evaluation in adult and pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy.

papers.title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. The Dreem3 replicated some established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Although not all expected age-related associations reached statistical significance, like total sleep time and sleep efficiency, effect estimates were largely in the expected direction. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

papers.title: Macroscale dynamics of EEG microstates constitute the periodic and aperiodic features of the neural power spectrum
papers.abstract: The global signal characteristics of scalp-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) are composed of periodic oscillatory rhythms and aperiodic broadband fluctuations that together comprise the neural power spectrum. Spectral decomposition of these features has long served as the primary window into the macroscale characteristics of human brain activity. Here, we propose that the primary periodic rhythms and majority share of broadband spectral power within the brain's dominant frequencies are the frequency-domain representations of the dynamics of EEG microstates. Microstates are characterized by a small repertoire of topographic voltage configurations that each reflect the momentary functional state of the cortex, and it is their time-domain dynamics that mathematically constitute periodic and aperiodic spectral features. We isolated and removed the spatial projections of distinct microstate configurations from high-density EEG using orthogonal subspace projection applied to both the surface scalp recordings and their modeled cortical generators to computationally test this dependency. Spectral parameterization of the residual power spectral density revealed that removing these spatial projections strongly attenuated alpha and theta rhythms and features of the aperiodic 1/f background. Selectively removing specific microstate configurations also demonstrated that each configuration aligned with spatially specific oscillatory and aperiodic 1/f components. Furthermore, correlational analyses of microstate temporal dynamics demonstrated that the average duration and temporal persistence of microstates strongly correlate with periodic alpha power, theta power, and the aperiodic 1/f background. Our findings suggest that dominant periodic and aperiodic spectral features are more accurately understood as the frequency-domain expressions of the dynamics of EEG microstates.

papers.title: Environmental enrichment during adolescence ameliorates anxiety-related corticosterone, enhances memory, and is associated with changes in regional dopamine levels in the Wistar Kyoto rat, a putative model of endogenous depression.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period in neurodevelopment marked by heightened plasticity, cognitive enhancement, and susceptibility to stress-induced impairments. The Wistar-Kyoto rat displays anxiety- and depressive-like behaviours, dysregulated stress responses and cognitive deficits, making it ideal for studying the effect of environmental interventions. Here, effects of environmental enrichment (EE) were assessed on anxiety, cognition, peripheral markers and monoaminergic levels. Male and female WKY were exposed to EE from postnatal day 22 onwards and assessed as mid-, late adolescents or young adults using novel object recognition, elevated plus maze (EPM), and radial arm maze paradigms. Serum and brain dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and corticosterone (CORT) were quantified by ELISA and LC-MS/MS. Results demonstrated that EE enhanced recognition memory (p < 0.0001) in adolescents, and spatial memory (p < 0.0001) in young adults. Peripherally, CORT decreased. During mid-adolescence, EE increased prefrontal DA (p = 0.006) in females, and caudate putamen and Nucleus accumbens DA in both sexes. During late adolescence, EE increased caudate putamen DA (p = 0.006) in females and Nucleus accumbens DA in males (p = 0.03). Correlational analyses indicated that recognition memory was associated with prefrontal and striatal DA levels, while anxiety correlated with CORT levels and prefrontal 5-HT levels, indicating that EE may enhance cognition and reduce anxiety with associated changes in DA levels. Given that the WKY depicts some face, construct and predictive validities of anxiety and depression, EE-based strategies may offer therapeutic potential for stress-related cognitive and emotional disorders in adolescents.

papers.title: A Breathable Nanomesh-Textile Electrode Interface for Integrated Multimodal Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiology requires electrodes that are skin-conformal, breathable, mechanically stable, and reliably connected to electronics. Existing dry electrodes address parts of this challenge, but the interface between soft electrodes and wearable electronics remains a major source of motion artifacts, open-circuit failure, and poor long-term usability. Here, we introduce a duo-electrode interface that separates the functions of skin contact and electronic interconnection. An electrospun nanomesh serves as a tattoo electrode that conforms intimately to the skin, while a compressible conductive taffeta-foam fabric electrode embedded in a garment provides stable electrical coupling to textile-routed electronics. This architecture preserves the advantages of skin-conformal electrodes while avoiding fragile connections to electronics. We integrate the interface into a bodysuit and eyemask platform for multimodal monitoring of ECG, EMG, EOG, and body position using a centralized electronics module. The system maintains reliable signal acquisition under body motion and muscle activation, with performance comparable to or better than that of commercial hydrogel electrodes. By bridging breathable electrodes with textile-based routing, the proposed duo-electrode strategy establishes a practical method for scalable, comfortable, and long-duration wearable bioelectronic monitoring. This approach may be broadly useful for remote healthcare, rehabilitation, sleep studies, human-machine interfaces, and personalized physiological sensing.

papers.title: Hypothalamic astrocytes fine-tune the signals governing metabolism.
papers.abstract: Astrocytes are known to have key roles in the neuroendocrine control of metabolism. The spectrum of actions of this cell population continues to expand as their heterogeneity is deciphered and new study approaches are employed. Astrocytes were first implicated in metabolic control when they were shown to participate in hypothalamic inflammation induced by high-fat diets, which leads to complications such as continued weight gain and glucose intolerance. In addition to their participation in pathophysiological processes associated with poor nutrition and obesity, these glial cells are now accepted as fundamental players in the physiological control of energy homeostasis. Along with their effect on neurons controlling appetite and energy expenditure, glial cells are implicitly involved in the generation of circadian rhythms, including eating and sleep patterns that affect metabolism and may link metabolism with other neuroendocrine systems such as puberty. The evolving concepts regarding astrocytes in metabolic control, including their participation in responses to currently used obesity drugs, highlight them as potential therapeutic targets. Here, we review advances in our understanding of how astrocytes participate in these processes, describe the mechanisms involved and discuss future directions.

papers.title: Time of day metabolism and endocrine regulation of immune health.
papers.abstract: The immune system is a dynamic, energy-dependent network regulated by temporal biology. Advances in circadian biology have enabled the synchronizing of critical immune parameters such as metabolism, endocrine secretions, surveillance, tissue repair, and adaptation to environmental cycles. Here, we propose a metabolomic, and endocrine, chromodynamic model of immune health, based on time-of-day rhythms. Immune resilience is defined by synchronization among three groups of oscillators i) the central circadian clocks, ii) food-entrainable metabolic oscillators, iii) peripheral cellular clocks. The model provides a framework to optimize these interconnected systems to maintain metabolic efficiency, minimize unnecessary inflammation, and enable precise immune responses through temporal gating. External factors of modern lifestyle disruptions, including irregular feeding patterns, sleep deprivation, and chronic stress, induce internal circadian desynchrony, contributing to persistent low-grade inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, immune aging, and chronic non-communicable diseases. We propose that immune health is characterized not merely by the absence of disease, but by stable circadian phase coherence, low inflammatory noise, and adaptive immune resilience. We have listed some chrono-biomarkers of metabolomic and endocrine parameters that may provide a functional assessment of immune resilience, defined by inflammatory tone, immune adaptability, metabolic integrity, and repair capacity. This framework integrates chronobiology, endocrine and immunometabolism to shift medicine from reactive disease management toward proactive assessment and restoration of biological resilience.

papers.title: LBSNet: Lightweight Brain State Modeling via Learnable Spectral Prototypes for EEG-Based Fatigue Detection
papers.abstract: EEG-based fatigue detection requires modeling spectral information across bands and its temporal variation. Recent methods combine multi-band modeling with adaptive temporal processing, yet how spectral structure across bands should influence the contribution of each temporal interval remains insufficiently explored. We propose LBSNet, a lightweight network that uses prototype-based brain-state modeling to link local spectral structure with temporal aggregation. LBSNet extracts compact multi-band features through band-specific temporal convolution, shared spatial projections, and cross-band recalibration. Within each window, relative spectral activity is encoded as a normalized descriptor and softly matched to learnable spectral prototypes. Prototype assignments and learned prototype importance jointly determine temporal weights for power aggregation, allowing the spectral pattern of each window to guide its contribution to the prediction. Subject-independent experiments on SEED-VIG and SADT show that LBSNet outperforms seven baselines while maintaining low computational cost. Ablation and visualization analyses support prototype-guided temporal weighting, while the learned prototypes reveal a gradual redistribution of relative cross-band spectral states with increasing fatigue. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zy0929/LBSNet.

papers.title: Time-dependent efficacy of vitamin D3 against chronic stress-induced behavioral and circadian deficits via the hepatic VDR-clock axis.
papers.abstract: Vitamin D3 (VitD3) is an essential fat-soluble micronutrient that protects against chronic stress-related disorders through its neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects. Major depressive disorder is accompanied by circadian rhythm (CR) disruption, and evidence from chrono-nutrition studies suggests that nutrient effects are strongly influenced by administration timing. However, whether VitD3 efficacy against chronic stress depends on intervention timing remains unclear. This study assessed the chrono-nutrition potential of VitD3 in a mouse model of chronic stress. Mice subjected to 4 weeks of chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) received daily VitD3 either in the morning (AM) or evening (PM). VitD3 treatment mitigated CUMS-induced behavioral impairments, neuroinflammation, and neuronal damage in a time-dependent manner, with superior outcomes observed with PM administration. PM administration enhanced anxiety- and depression-like behaviors, hippocampal integrity, TNF-α levels, sleep duration, and serotonin synthesis. Mechanistically, PM administration more effectively restored hepatic Vdr rhythmic oscillation, coupled with re-synchronization of the core clock network. Genetic validation in Caenorhabditis elegans further supported the essential role of VDR in circadian restoration. This study is the first to reveal the time-dependent antidepressant effects of VitD3 and identify the VDR-circadian clock axis as the underlying mechanism. These findings highlight the importance of intervention timing for VitD3 efficacy and support precision nutrition strategies aligned with CR for stress disorders.

papers.title: Evening amber-lensed glasses in combination with a prescribed wake time advance circadian timing in adolescents with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder.
papers.abstract: We tested whether wearing amber glasses during evening hours and a stable wake time advances circadian and sleep timing of adolescent patients with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWPD). Adolescents (14.3-18.1 years; n = 36 randomized) with DSWPD completed a 3-week study. Dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) was measured after 1 week of habitual sleep/wake. During the next 2 weeks, participants were randomized to one of two groups: the treatment group wore amber-lensed glasses, and a control group wore clear-lensed glasses nightly, starting 7 h before midpoint of baseline sleep, and ending at self-selected bedtime or for 7 h, whichever was shorter. Treatment group participants were additionally instructed to wake at their average baseline school-day wake time (± 15 min). Final DLMO was measured at the end. The treatment group advanced 40 ± 84 min and the control group delayed - 29 ± 50 min [t(26) = - 2.63, p = .01]. Despite circadian phase changes, weeknight sleep onset and duration remained stable with the amber glasses + stable wake intervention. Weekday wake-up time did not differ between groups; however, the Treatment group woke earlier on weekends during the glasses weeks compared to the Control group [t(25) = 4.13, p < .001], resulting in more stable sleep times across the week. Amber glasses in the evening with fixed wake times shifted circadian phase earlier among adolescents with DSWPD. Although sleep onset did not advance, sleep timing was more consistent across the week. This strategy represents a readily implemented cost-effective intervention to advance the circadian clock and reduce social jet lag in a difficult-to-treat young patient group. Additional directives may be needed to effect other sleep-related outcomes. Current knowledge/study rationale Adolescent patients with DSWPD are at high risk for deleterious sleep-related outcomes. Feasible and effective treatment interventions are sparse. Amber glasses timed strategically in the evening with a fixed wake time was associated with circadian phase advances and reduced sleep variability. This intervention is cost-effective and readily implemented. Since physiological changes did not translate into changes in additional sleep/wake behaviors, however, future treatment approaches need to be further refined and delineated. papers.title: Circadian rhythm and cancer-related pain: a systematic review of preclinical and clinical evidence.
papers.abstract: Cancer-related pain and neuropathy are common complications that substantially affect quality of life. Circadian rhythms regulate biological processes involved in pain and treatment response; however, evidence linking circadian biology and treatment timing with cancer-related pain and neuropathy remains limited and heterogeneous, and the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. This systematic review aimed to evaluate these relationships and their potential biological mechanisms and clinical implications across clinical and preclinical studies. PRISMA-guided systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251174524). PubMed and Web of Science were searched for original human and preclinical studies published up to October 20, 2025. Eligible studies evaluated circadian rhythms, clock genes, or circadian-based treatment timing in relation to cancer- or treatment-related pain, neuropathy, or analgesic response. Direct pain-related and indirect neuropathy outcomes were synthesized separately. Risk of bias was assessed using JBI tools for human studies and SYRCLE for preclinical studies. Thirty-nine studies were included: 35 human (89.7%) and 4 preclinical studies (10.3%). Most populations included mixed cancer types (10/39, 25.6%). Cohort or observational studies represented 38.5% and clinical trials represented 28.2%, with 16/39 (41%) studies published between 2015 and 2025. Clinical findings were heterogeneous, with temporal variation reported for cancer-related pain and analgesic requirements, while chronotherapy studies suggested potential reductions in treatment-related neuropathy and neurotoxicity, representing indirect pain-related evidence. Potential mechanisms were reported or discussed in 15/35 (42.9%) human studies and were largely hypothesis-generating, involving HPA-axis/cortisol dysregulation, drug pharmacokinetics, and metabolism, inflammatory signaling, and circadian-regulatory pathways; direct clinical clock-gene evidence was limited to RORA. Four preclinical studies provided experimental evidence implicating clock genes (PER2, BMAL1, and REV-ERBα/β), oxidative stress, neuronal injury, drug metabolism, and neuroinflammatory (IL-6/LCN2) pathways. Methodological quality was limited, with high risk of bias in 10/15 (67%) cohort studies and 8/11 (73%) clinical trials and high or unclear risk across several preclinical domains. Current evidence suggests a potential relationship between circadian biology and cancer- and treatment-related pain, analgesic response, and neuropathy. Clinical findings remain heterogeneous, human mechanistic evidence is predominantly hypothesis-generating, and experimental evidence remains limited. Prospective mechanistic studies are needed to support future circadian-informed approaches for cancer pain management. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251174524, identifier CRD420251174524.

papers.title: Cortical depth EEG-fMRI at 7T: Experimental setup and analysis pipeline to elucidate generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations.
papers.abstract: Alpha band (8-13 Hz) electroencephalography (EEG) oscillations are central to cognition, but their generating mechanisms are poorly understood. Most laminar studies investigating origins of alpha oscillations rely on invasive animal intracranial recordings. To relate these findings to human alpha generation, non-invasive techniques need to be developed. Ultra-high-field (UHF, 7T) laminar functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables cortical depth resolved brain responses, and, combined with simultaneous EEG, offers new insight into human alpha generation mechanisms. This work presents a framework for studying the generating mechanisms of electrophysiological signals non-invasively in humans using simultaneous EEG laminar fMRI. Data were acquired on 10 participants during an eyes-closed/eyes-open paradigm. In 9 of 10 participants, the quality of EEG and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) fMRI data were sufficient to observe a significant negative correlation between EEG alpha power and the BOLD signal in visual cortex grey matter. To improve depth specificity and mitigate pial-surface BOLD signal increases due to draining veins, we applied "deveining". The effects of each of the deveining analysis steps on the cortical depth profiles of the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were studied. The largest effect arose from excluding voxels in the tissue immediately surrounding veins. After deveining, the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were significantly weaker in the middle cortical depths than in superficial and deep depths. This depth dependence was absent when modelling the task with a boxcar regressor rather than EEG alpha power, suggesting specificity to spontaneous electrophysiological (alpha) fluctuations. In conclusion, we have established a method to non-invasively interrogate the origins of electrophysiological signals. Our alpha-BOLD depth profiles during the eyes-open/eyes-closed task (strongest correlations in superficial and deep layers) are consistent with activity in cortical depths typically associated with feedback/top-down processing, but we cannot definitively demonstrate causality from these data.

papers.title: Circadian Clock Coordination of the Notch-to-Wnt Signaling Switch Promotes Regenerative Myogenesis
papers.abstract: Regenerative deficits of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) contribute to progressive muscle loss in muscular dystrophy. Successful regenerative repair requires a Notch to Wnt switch to allow MuSC expansion and myogenic differentiation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Leveraging complementary genetic and pharmacological approaches, here we identify the circadian clock as a key regulator of the Notch to Wnt signaling transition to promote regeneration with therapeutic potential for dystrophic disease. Circadian clock activity marks cycling myogenic progenitors during muscle regeneration, and clock induction occurs in concert with Notch activation. We identify that key components of the Notch pathway are direct transcriptional targets of the clock that were induced by clock activation. Mechanistically, clock coordination of Notch and Wnt signaling promoted MuSC proliferative expansion while facilitating myogenic progression during regeneration. Importantly, this clock-regulated mechanism was preserved in dystrophin-deficient mouse and human myoblasts, and clock-activating compounds enhanced regenerative myogenesis in dystrophic muscle. Collectively, our findings uncover a circadian clock-controlled mechanism that orchestrates regenerative signaling transition with potential for therapeutic targeting to restore regenerative capacity in dystrophic disease.

papers.title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result
papers.abstract: Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure prediction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. We asked how much short-horizon warning survives a pre-specified, locked evaluation. Continuous video-EEG from 21 monitored children (1315 h) formed the development cohort. A statistical-process-control warning method, evaluated under a written protocol, detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. papers.title: Serial Amplitude-Integrated Electroencephalography and the Burdjalov Score in Preterm Infants: A Prospective Longitudinal Bedside Study in the Neonatal Care Unit.
papers.abstract: Preterm birth interrupts occurs during a critical period of cortical organization, and objective bedside tools for tracking functional maturation remain limited. The aim of this study was to assess the interobserver reproducibility of the Burdjalov score and to characterize longitudinal electrocortical maturation in preterm infants up to term-equivalent age. Prospective longitudinal observational study in a neonatal intensive care unit and an intermediate care unit, data collected from September 2021 to August 2023. Infants born before 35 weeks of gestation, stratified by gestational age (GA) at birth (<28, 28-30, 31-34 weeks), who underwent serial two-channel amplitude-integrated electroencephalography until term-equivalent age or discharge. Term newborns with a single recording served as physiological reference. Outcomes measures were the Burdjalov scores, rated independently by three blinded observers was. Agreement was assessed by the intraclass correlation coefficient and kappa, maturation by linear regression on corrected GA, and time to a maximal score of 13 by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Forty-eight preterm infants (125 recordings) and 29 term newborns were included. Total-score agreement was excellent (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.98, 95% confidence interval 0.98-0.99), with kappa ≥0.60 for all components. Scores rose continuously with corrected GA in all strata, approaching maximal values around 37 weeks and matching the term reference. Time to maturity did not differ between strata (log-rank P = 0.823). Serial amplitude-integrated electroencephalography scored with the Burdjalov scale is an objective, highly reproducible method for monitoring electrocortical maturation in preterm infants. Functional maturation follows corrected age rather than GA at birth, providing a bedside reference for detecting atypical maturational trajectories.

papers.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Sleep Disturbances: A Narrative Review of Bidirectional Mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease in which sleep disturbances are common and closely linked to pain, fatigue, mood symptoms, physical dysfunction, and disease activity. This narrative review synthesizes clinical and mechanistic evidence for a bidirectional relationship between RA and impaired sleep while distinguishing diagnosed sleep disorders from transdiagnostic sleep symptoms. RA-related inflammation, pain, stiffness, and psychological comorbidity may impair sleep through peripheral-to-central inflammatory signaling, altered monoamine metabolism, circadian disruption, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction, autonomic hyperarousal, and central sensitization. Conversely, insufficient or fragmented sleep may disrupt immune and circadian homeostasis, amplify pro-inflammatory signaling and pain sensitivity, and thereby worsen RA symptoms and possibly disease activity. However, much of the available evidence is cross-sectional, based on patient-reported sleep, or derived from small treatment studies, so direct causality and the independent contribution of individual pathways remain uncertain. Evidence from cytokine-blocking and sleep-directed interventions suggests potential benefit, but improvements may be mediated through changes in pain, fatigue, mood, and inflammatory activity. Age, sex, adiposity, medications, depression, anxiety, and sleep-disorder phenotype further modify these associations. Clinically, RA care should distinguish insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome, circadian problems, and non-diagnostic sleep symptoms, then combine optimized RA and pain management with disorder-specific sleep treatment. Longitudinal multimodal cohorts and adequately powered trials using both patient-reported and objective sleep outcomes are priorities.

papers.title: A sex-specific modification of the SARA questionnaire for obstructive sleep apnea screening: Comparative validation against six other tools in the HypnoLaus cohort.
papers.abstract: and objectivesObstructive sleep apnea is significantly underdiagnosed in women, partly because existing screening tools were developed in male-predominant cohorts and may fail to capture female-specific clinical presentations. We used the HypnoLaus population-based cohort (n = 1540; 718 women, 822 men) to evaluate seven OSA screening tools in this cross-sectional study and assessed whether adding menopausal status to SARA enhances diagnostic accuracy. Moderate-to-severe OSA was defined as AHI ≥ 15 events per hour on polysomnography. The study included 1540 participants (718 women, 822 men). NoSAS and the updated SARA demonstrated the highest overall discriminative performance, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs), 0.741 (95% CI, 0.718-0.764) and 0.693 (95% CI, 0.669-0.716), respectively, followed by original SARA (AUC, 0.684), Berlin (0.635), SONA (0.579), STOP-Bang (0.575), and ESS (0.507). Incorporation of menopausal status improved discrimination of SARA in women (AUC 0.675 vs. 0.627; p = 0.001). Although NoSAS showed the highest overall AUC, updated SARA performed more consistently across sex-, age-, and BMI-defined phenotypes. In women ≤55 years, updated SARA showed higher discrimination than NoSAS (AUC 0.616 vs. 0.509; p = 0.014), and in lean women (BMI <25 kg/m2), updated SARA detected cases that NoSAS missed (sensitivity 42.3% vs. 0%). Sex-related differences affect OSA screening. Incorporating menopausal status into SARA improved OSA detection in women. At the same time, anthropometry-weighted tools such as NoSAS performed poorly in younger, leaner women, underscoring the limitations of anthropometry-based screening in these phenotypes.

papers.title: Multimodal EEG-fNIRS complexity analysis can reveal the neurovascular coupling change with aging.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate age-related changes in neurovascular coupling (NVC) function of the brain using a multimodal electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) approach combined with nonlinear entropy analysis. The study included 20 young adults and 20 older adults. We simultaneously recorded EEG and fNIRS data during four cognitive tasks (auditory attention task, verbal fluency task, upper limb motor task, and recognition memory task). We calculated sample entropy (SampEn) and conditional entropy (CondEn) for five EEG frequency sub-bands (Delta: 1-4 Hz, Theta: 4-8 Hz, Alpha: 8-12 Hz, Beta: 12-30 Hz, Gamma: 30-40 Hz) as well as for fNIRS signals (oxygenated hemoglobin and deoxygenated hemoglobin, HbO and HbR) to quantify neural and hemodynamic complexity of brain activity. Additionally, cross-sample entropy (Cross-SampEn) and cross-conditional entropy (Cross-CondEn) between EEG and fNIRS signals were computed to evaluate NVC function. Group differences were assessed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with age group as the fixed factor and sex and years of education as covariates. Older adults showed higher EEG SampEn or CondEn in selected frequency bands during the auditory attention task and the encoding and recognition phases of the recognition memory task. For fNIRS, older adults showed lower HbO SampEn during memory recognition. Cross-modal analysis showed lower beta-HbR Cross-SampEn during the left upper limb motor task and higher theta-HbR Cross-SampEn during memory encoding in older adults. Aging is associated with task-specific alterations in neural complexity, hemodynamic complexity, and the cross-modal temporal relationship between EEG and fNIRS signals. These findings suggest that age-related changes in NVC-related dynamics are better characterized as dynamic reorganization rather than a uniform enhancement or impairment, and support the potential of multimodal entropy analysis for characterizing age-related neurovascular coupling change.

papers.title: Multiscale EEG network alterations in adolescents with depressive symptoms: static-dynamic connectivity, topological features, and exploratory scalp-level network hubs.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for brain network development and a vulnerable stage for the emergence of depressive symptoms Although altered brain connectivity has been reported in depression, the multiscale organization of resting-state EEG networks in adolescents with depressive symptoms (ADS) remains insufficiently understood. In particular, conventional network analyses are often constrained by fixed thresholding strategies and single-level observations, which may obscure scale-specific and topology-related abnormalities. Eyes-closed resting-state EEG data were collected from 96 adolescents with depressive symptoms and 154 healthy controls. A data-driven adaptive thresholding strategy was used to construct subject-specific brain functional networks. Static functional connectivity, dynamic functional connectivity, and higher-order topological features were analyzed across macro-, meso-, and micro-scale levels. A multidimensional abnormality convergence matrix was further constructed to explore the spatial correspondence between network abnormalities and exploratory scalp-level neuromodulation hubs. ADS showed scale-dependent abnormalities in brain network organization. At the macro- and meso-scale levels, abnormalities were mainly characterized by theta-band static hyperconnectivity, particularly involving central-region networks, together with reduced dynamic transition flexibility involving prefrontal systems. Micro-scale analysis further localized these alterations to specific connections and nodes. Static connectivity abnormalities were mainly observed along the midline prefrontal-central axis, including Fp1/Fz-FCz connections, whereas dynamic instability was mainly found in right prefrontal-occipital pathways, including Fp2/F4-Oz connections. Higher-order topological analysis indicated vulnerability of right prefrontal nodes, particularly Fp2 and F4. The convergence matrix showed spatial overlap between abnormal network features and the approximate scalp projections of prefrontal neuromodulation sites, while also identifying FCz and Oz as additional nodes that may warrant further investigation. This study provides a multiscale EEG network characterization of adolescents with depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that ADS-related network alterations may involve coexisting compensatory connectivity changes, reduced dynamic flexibility, and focal topological vulnerability. These results may help refine network-level features and provide hypothesis-generating computational references for future studies exploring individualized neuromodulation strategies in adolescents with depressive symptoms.

papers.title: Intermittent hypoxia-driven gut microbial and metabolic remodeling in obstructive sleep apnea: mechanisms and evidence across target organs.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) exposes tissues to recurrent intermittent hypoxia (IH) and is associated with multisystem morbidity. Growing evidence implicates the gut microbiota and microbial metabolism in these consequences, but their contribution to target-organ injury remains uncertain. This narrative review examines how IH remodels the intestinal environment and evaluates the evidence linking these changes to systemic injury, distinguishing preclinical experimental findings from human clinical observations. IH can disturb intestinal oxygen homeostasis, impair epithelial barrier function, and alter microbial and host-microbial metabolic pathways involving short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and trimethylamine N-oxide. These changes may influence distant tissues through metabolic signaling and immune activation. Preclinical studies support a functional microbial contribution to selected cardiovascular, metabolic, and neurocognitive phenotypes, but mechanistic resolution and applicability vary with exposure conditions, diet, and host background. Human studies remain predominantly observational and do not establish microbial mediation of OSA-related organ injury. Overall, the gut microbiota is best regarded as a context-dependent contributor and amplifier of IH-related injury, rather than a universal mediator. A focus on microbial function and host-microbial co-metabolism may be more informative than inconsistent taxonomic signatures. Longitudinal studies and targeted interventions are needed to establish clinical relevance and determine whether microbiome-directed approaches can complement established OSA treatment.

papers.title: Accelerometry-Derived REM Sleep Behavior Disorder Score Is Associated with Incident Parkinson's Disease in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Estimating Parkinson's disease (PD) risk years before diagnosis remains an unmet need. We applied a validated machine learning classifier for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) detection to 7-day wrist accelerometry data in 87,975 UK Biobank participants followed for 10 years. Participants in the highest RBD risk stratum (>99th percentile) had an approximately fivefold increased hazard of incident PD compared with the lowest-risk group (0-90th percentile), with a dose-dependent relationship across the full score distribution. Among non-converters, higher RBD-classifier scores were associated with baseline cognitive deficits and greater burden of autonomic and psychiatric prodromal features. The association with incident PD remained independent of PD polygenic risk score, while RBD-classifier score and genetic risk were synergistic. The combined high-risk group achieved a positive likelihood ratio of 7.91, approximately threefold higher than questionnaire-based RBD screening. At this High-risk threshold over the 10-year horizon, the classifier showed a sensitivity of 7.4%, specificity of 99.2%, positive predictive value of 7.5%, and negative predictive value of 99.2% for incident PD (N=50,816). These findings support wrist accelerometry as a scalable, high-specificity approach for prodromal PD risk enrichment.

papers.title: Sex-related clinical profiles in obstructive sleep apnea: An integrated clinical, sleep study, and drug-induced sleep endoscopy analysis.
papers.abstract: Sex-related differences in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) are well recognized, but their association with dynamic upper airway collapse remains poorly characterized. To characterize sex-related clinical profiles in OSA through the integrated assessment of clinical characteristics, sleep study parameters, and drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) findings. This retrospective study compared clinical profiles, sleep parameters, collapse patterns, airway reversibility, and treatment recommendations in 767 patients undergoing DISE. Women were older and more frequently reported insomnia and mood disorders, whereas men had higher body mass index, larger tonsils, and higher Mallampati scores. Sleep study differences were also observed: men exhibited longer apneas, higher apnea-to-hypopnea ratios, and more positional OSA. Respiratory event clustering suggestive of REM-related OSA was more frequent in women, although REM sleep was not EEG-confirmed. DISE demonstrated that obstruction was more frequent in men at all assessed levels, including palatal concentric collapse (62.5% vs 40.7%). Complete resolution with jaw thrust was more frequent in women (30.2% vs 18.4%). Mandibular advancement therapy was more commonly recommended for women, whereas surgery was more frequently recommended for men. Findings in this DISE-selected cohort suggest a predominantly anatomy-driven pattern in men and a potentially more functionally modulated profile in women, supporting the integration of sex-related characteristics into personalized treatment selection.

papers.title: Evidence of high rates of burnout symptoms in a cohort with cluster headache.
papers.abstract: Cluster headache is a debilitating primary headache disorder. During active bouts, headache attacks occur daily and can last up to 3 h. Besides the excruciating pain, the disorder can greatly impact a patient's mental health, sleep, and life quality. The reoccurring attacks as well as sleep problems may lead to energy depletion and burnout symptoms, which can limit a person's ability to participate in society to the extent they would like to. Our aim was to investigate the extent of burnout symptoms in a Swedish cluster headache cohort using a cross-sectional approach. We further wanted to study if burnout symptoms can be linked to disease status-and if sex, lifestyle factors, or any specific clinical characteristics may be linked to change in burnout symptoms. Between January 2024 and September 2025, the Shirom-Melamed Burnout Questionnaire was sent out via the Research Electronic Data Capture platform to 839 study participants with cluster headache. Global scores from the questionnaire were compared between study participants in active bout and remission. Likewise, the scores were analyzed between participants whose remission period had lasted longer than 5 years (long-term) compared to less than 5 years (short-term). Lifestyle and clinical factors were further analyzed in study participants with high Shirom-Melamed Burnout Questionnaire scores (global score >3.75). The total number of individuals included in the analysis was 373/839 (44.5%). Scores above threshold (>3.75) were recorded in 65.9% (58/88) of study participants in an active bout compared to 37.5% (90/240) in the remission group (odds ratio [OR] = 3.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.93-5.38; p < 0.001). Participants in short-term remission similarly had a higher percentage of scores above threshold compared to participants in long-term remission (42.0% [73/174] vs. 22.2% [12/54], OR = 2.53, 95% CI = 1.25-5.14; p = 0.009). Participants with burnout scores above 3.75 were more likely to be females (OR = 3.25, 95% CI = 2.04-5.19; pcorrected <0.001) and report sleep deprivation as an attack trigger (OR = 2.24, 95% CI = 1.32-3.82; pcorrected = 0.034). Participants with cluster headache in our Swedish cohort reported higher scores for burnout symptoms, particularly during active bout. For participants in remission, the burnout symptoms score was inversely correlated to the number of years since their last active headache bout. When managing cluster headache in a clinical setting, it should be taken into consideration that this patient group has a substantial risk for developing burnout symptoms both in and out of an active bout. Future studies should evaluate how to best support patients with cluster headache handling exhaustion and promote recovery to improve their quality of life.

papers.title: MACS: mild by definition, challenging by nature.
papers.abstract: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) is the most frequent form of cortisol excess in patients with adrenal incidentalomas. Although it lacks the classical phenotype of overt Cushing's syndrome, MACS is increasingly recognized as a clinically relevant condition associated with multisystem complications rather than a benign biochemical finding. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnostic limitations, and management of MACS, with particular focus on cardiometabolic, skeletal, muscular, neuropsychiatric, frailty-related, reproductive, and emerging microbiome-related consequences. Chronic exposure to low-grade cortisol excess is being recognized as a factor associated with hypertension, disorders of glucose metabolism, dyslipidemia, increased cardiovascular risk, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, skeletal fragility, impaired muscle function, frailty, sleep and circadian disturbances, cognitive and mood alterations, hypogonadism, and possible changes in gut microbiota. The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, but its interpretation is limited by assay variability, medication interference, comorbidities, and imperfect reflection of long-term tissue glucocorticoid exposure. Emerging approaches, including steroid profiling, hair cortisol/cortisone, salivary cortisone, inflammatory indices, metabolomic tools, and exploratory biomarkers related to microbial metabolites, may improve risk stratification in the future but remain investigational. Management should be individualized. Adrenalectomy may benefit selected patients with unilateral disease and clinically relevant cortisol-related comorbidities, whereas evidence supporting pharmacological therapy remains limited. MACS should be regarded as a heterogeneous multisystem condition requiring structured clinical assessment and individualized management. Prospective studies are needed to define clinically meaningful endpoints, refine diagnostic thresholds, and identify patients most likely to benefit from intervention.

papers.title: Habitual sleep duration and spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage: a prospective UK Biobank cohort study with supporting hospital-based neurosurgical data.
papers.abstract: Abnormal sleep duration has been associated with stroke, but evidence specific to spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) remains limited. We conducted a two-part observational study. The prospective UK Biobank analysis included 314,236 participants free of sICH at baseline, among whom 1,387 developed incident sICH. The supporting cross-sectional hospital analysis included 312 patients with imaging-confirmed sICH and 515 non-ICH neurosurgical controls from Jinjiang Municipal Hospital. Habitual sleep duration was categorized as short (<7 h/day), normal (7-9 h/day), or long (>9 h/day). Cox proportional hazards models [hazard ratios (HRs)] and logistic regression [odds ratios (ORs)] were used, together with restricted cubic splines, additional adjustment for medications, blood pressure, and indicators of prevalent ill health, and multiple imputation of missing data. A systemic inflammatory marker score and interaction analyses with false-discovery-rate correction were examined as secondary, exploratory analyses. Compared with normal sleep, short and long sleep were associated with higher incident sICH risk in the UK Biobank [adjusted HRs 1.14 (95% CI 1.03-1.26) and 1.55 (1.15-2.09)]; the short-sleep association was modest and less robust in sensitivity analyses. Corresponding cross-sectional ORs in the hospital dataset were 1.49 (1.04-2.13) and 2.05 (1.17-3.59), respectively. Restricted cubic splines suggested U-shaped associations in both datasets, with the lowest estimated hazard or odds at approximately 7-8 h/day. Estimates were similar after additional confounder adjustment (HRs 1.10 and 1.43 for short and long sleep, respectively) and multiple imputation (HRs 1.13 and 1.50, respectively). No interaction, including with inflammatory marker burden, remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction, and adjustment for the marker score changed the estimates only modestly. Both short and long sleep duration were associated with higher incident sICH risk in the UK Biobank and higher odds of sICH in the hospital dataset, with stronger and more consistent associations observed for long sleep. Systemic inflammatory markers neither explained nor reliably modified these associations, and because long sleep may partly reflect prevalent ill health, the long-sleep association warrants cautious interpretation. papers.title: Side-to-side and other complex head movements as ictal signs in epilepsy: A video-EEG case series and review of literature.
papers.abstract: Side-to-side head shaking is often considered a distinctive clinical sign that differentiates functional seizures from epileptic seizures; however, it may also occur as an ictal phenomenon in focal epilepsy. We retrospectively reviewed all video-telemetry reports of patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing presurgical evaluation between 2015 and 2025. All reports were electronically screened for mentioning side-to-side or other complex head movements and the video-EEG of these patients was reviewed and included if associated with ictal EEG changes. Seventeen patients were identified who experienced 631 seizures in total, 201 of which included such movements (median: 2 per patient, range: 1-160). One patient (No. 5) accounted for 79% of these events and represented an outlier. Head movements were predominantly horizontal (93.5%), followed by mixed (5%) and rotatory (1.5%). While small-amplitude movements predominated overall, larger amplitudes were more frequent after excluding the outlier case. In six patients, head movements were the initial observed feature of seizure semiology and typically represented a brief component of the seizure, although prolonged in the outlier case. Interrater agreement ranged from fair to good across semiological variables. Presumed epileptogenic zones were heterogenous, including frontal, temporal, anterior quadrant, and hemispheric regions. Ictal side-to-side and other complex head movements can occur in focal epilepsies but lack localizing or lateralizing value. They likely reflect seizure propagation and involvement of broader neuronal circuits. Further studies are needed to clarify their mechanisms and clinical significance.

papers.abstract: Employed family caregivers of individuals with cognitive impairment often need to balance work responsibilities, caregiving tasks, and their own daily lives. Short sleep duration (<6 h/day) was also associated with a higher prevalence of psychological distress, whereas working hours and caregiving duration were not significantly associated with psychological distress after multivariable adjustment. Limited restorative free time may therefore serve as a potential marker of psychological distress in this population. papers.title: Differences in pulse oximetry saturation from sea level to high altitude among subjects with and without respiratory disease. A population-based, cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Oxygen saturation (SpO2) is used to detect hypoxemia and guide oxygen therapy, but its interpretation varies with altitude, age, and lung disease. Although >500 million people live at ≥1,500 m, population-based data comparing SpO2 across altitudes in adults with and without chronic respiratory disease are scarce. We aimed to compare SpO2 between these groups from sea level to 3,030 m, identify factors associated with SpO2, and describe SpO2 by altitude and age in adults without respiratory disease. We hypothesized that SpO2 would be lower in participants with respiratory disease, with differences increasing with altitude. PREPOCOL II is a population-based, cross-sectional study with a probabilistic, two-stage, clustered sampling design to estimate the prevalence and risk factors for respiratory disease among adults ≥40 years in Colombian cities at different altitudes (18-3030 m). All participants completed a standardized questionnaire, spirometry, and SpO2 measurement. Participants with respiratory disease (RDP), including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, chronic bronchitis, obstructive sleep apnea, and interstitial lung disease, were compared with controls using Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests, multivariable linear regression, and comparisons of altitude coefficients between groups. A total of 1146 RDP and 4613 controls were included. RDP were older, and had lower BMI and lung function. SpO2 was lower in RDP than in controls at all altitudes and decreased in both groups as altitude and age increased (p<0.001). In multivariable models, altitude showed the strongest association with SpO2 (standardized β -0.69 in controls and -0.71 in RDP), followed by age and BMI (and FEV1 in RDP). The decrease in SpO2 per unit of altitude was larger in RDP (B -1.15 vs. -0.80; difference p<0.001), and the between-group difference became evident at ~1,500 m (median 97.0% vs. 95.5%). Among lifelong residents living at altitudes from sea level to 3,030 m, SpO2 was lower in RDP than in controls. SpO2 decreased with altitude and age in both groups, with altitude being the variable most strongly associated with SpO2. SpO2 values should be interpreted in relation to specific altitude and age. In RDP, the lower SpO2 was most evident at altitudes of ~1,500 m and above.

papers.title: Circadian syndrome and headache accompanied by stomach pain among middle-aged and older Chinese adults: associations and the mediating role of frailty.
papers.abstract: Circadian syndrome (CircS) integrates metabolic abnormalities, short sleep duration, and depressive symptoms, and may reflect multidimensional circadian-related health dysregulation. Migraine is a disabling neurological disorder that is frequently accompanied by gastrointestinal symptoms, but evidence on the association between CircS and migraine-related symptom phenotypes in middle-aged and older adults remains limited. This study examined the associations between CircS and headache accompanied by stomach pain, a self-reported symptom co-occurrence phenotype, and explored the mediating role of frailty. Data were obtained from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. A total of 9,342 participants were included in the cross-sectional analysis, and 5,895 participants without headache accompanied by stomach pain at baseline were included in the longitudinal analysis. CircS was defined as the presence of at least four of seven components. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine the associations of CircS with prevalent and incident headache accompanied by stomach pain, respectively. Sensitivity analyses included complete-case analyses, a 2-year lag analysis, age-restricted analysis, propensity score matching, and E-value analysis. Time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves and bootstrap mediation analysis were also performed. CircS was associated with higher odds of prevalent headache accompanied by stomach pain after full adjustment (OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.14-1.67, p < 0.001). During follow-up, 969 participants developed incident headache accompanied by stomach pain. CircS was associated with an increased risk of incident headache accompanied by stomach pain (HR = 1.33, 95% CI: 1.16-1.51), and the risk increased with greater CircS component burden. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the main findings. CircS showed numerically higher discriminative ability than metabolic syndrome and individual CircS components. Frailty explained 19.72% of the association between CircS and incident headache accompanied by stomach pain (p < 0.001). Among middle-aged and older Chinese adults, CircS was associated with prevalent and incident headache accompanied by stomach pain, and frailty partially explained this association. As the outcome was based on self-reported symptom co-occurrence, it should not be equated with clinically diagnosed migraine.

papers.title: Quantifying Academic Risk Factors for Student Depression Using WHO Frameworks: Odds Ratios, SHAP Explainability, and Tipping Point Analysis
papers.abstract: Depression has become a serious concern for students worldwide. Aligned with the WHO Helping Adolescents Thrive (HAT) Guidelines and the Social Determinants of Health (SDoH) model, this study isolates five academically relevant factors- academic pressure, work/study hours, study satisfaction, sleep duration, and financial stress- from a dataset of 27,880 university students in India and quantifies their associations with depression. Unlike prior work that maximises classification accuracy, this study prioritises interpretability: logistic regression provides odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals, Random Forest (RF) and XGBoost rank predictors by feature importance, and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values extend the analysis to individual-level risk explanation. Sleep Duration is encoded as an ordinal integer (0-3) preserving its natural order, and Spearman correlations are computed on the original 27,880-row dataset prior to any resampling. SMOTE oversampling was applied exclusively to the training set, and performance was evaluated on the original imbalanced test set (n = 5,576). Both ensemble models achieve approximately 77-78% accuracy and an AUC of 0.845, confirmed by 5-fold pipeline cross-validation (CV AUC [~] 0.843). Academic pressure is the dominant risk factor (OR = 2.271; RF importance = 0.481; mean |SHAP| = 0.174), while study satisfaction (OR = 0.796) and sleep duration (OR = 0.835) are protective. Interaction analysis reveals how depression risk is amplified by low sleep, high financial stress, and extended study hours: under average conditions, the 50% risk threshold is crossed at Academic Pressure {approx} 3.04, and under compounded adverse conditions, this tipping point shifts to even lower pressure values. These findings provide data-driven thresholds aligned with WHO-endorsed modifiable determinants to support early detection and institutional counselling.

papers.title: Effect of neurofeedback-assisted mindfulness training on migraine severity, associated disability, sleep quality, and emotional distress: protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Migraine is a highly prevalent neurological disorder and a leading cause of worldwide disability, exerting significant clinical, social, and economic burdens. While pharmacological options exist, their efficacy is often limited by tolerability issues and risk of medication-overuse headache. Neurofeedback (NF) combined with mindfulness training has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological neuromodulation technique. However, clinical evidence in migraine management remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and small sample sizes. This study protocol aims to evaluate the efficacy of a Neurofeedback-Assisted Mindfulness Training Program (NAMTP) in adults with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine. This is a randomized, parallel-group, controlled clinical trial protocol. Sixty-six (N = 66) adults diagnosed with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine (5-14 monthly migraine days) will be recruited and randomized (1:1 ratio) into either the Intervention Group (IG: standard care plus NAMTP) or the Control Group (CG: standard routine care alone). The IG will undergo a 12-week home-based program consisting of 60 sessions (15-20 min each, 5 times per week) of mindfulness training assisted by the Muse® electroencephalography (EEG) headband. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, 12 weeks (post-intervention), and 24 weeks post-randomization. The powered primary outcome is the change in Monthly Migraine Days (MMDs). Secondary outcomes include migraine-associated disability (MIDAS), headache impact (HIT-6), sleep parameters (actigraphy and PSQI), quality of life (MSQ v.2), and mood symptoms (BDI-II and STAI-Y). This protocol addresses the urgent need for scalable, non-pharmacological therapies in migraine management. By combining objective neurophysiological monitoring with behavioral training within a rigorous randomized controlled framework, this trial will clarify whether NAMTP can reduce headache burden, optimize sleep patterns, and diminish affective distress. The findings are expected to provide standardized, actionable evidence regarding the integration of digital neurofeedback tools into routine clinical care for episodic migraine.Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07661888.

papers.title: Associations between the duration of outdoor sunlight exposure and the risk of developing 134 different diseases.
papers.abstract: Existing studies of sunlight exposure and health have mainly focused on specific organs, particularly the skin and eyes, while associations with other organs and systems remain largely unexplored. We aimed to comprehensively examine the associations between outdoor sunlight exposure duration and 134 diseases. Using UK Biobank data, summer and winter outdoor durations were collected by questionnaire, and average daily exposure was calculated as their arithmetic mean. Incident diseases were defined using 525 three-character ICD-10 codes. Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations, and restricted cubic splines assessed potential nonlinearity. Among 281,282 participants [mean (SD) age, 55.81 (8.07) years; 55.79% female], 1,115,346 incident cases occurred during a median follow-up of more than 13.4 years. After false discovery rate correction, sunlight exposure was associated with 36 diseases, with hazard ratios ranging from 0.914 to 1.086. For example, each additional hour of average exposure was associated with higher risks of malignant melanoma of the skin (HR = 1.052, 95% CI 1.012-1.094), obesity (1.039, 1.027-1.052), cerebrovascular diseases (1.028, 1.011-1.046), and osteoarthritis (1.042, 1.033-1.052), and lower risks of osteoporosis (0.975, 0.957-0.994), disorders of mineral metabolism (0.968, 0.944-0.992), and pressure ulcers (0.947, 0.916-0.979). Thirty diseases, including depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, arrhythmias, iron deficiency anemia, and kidney failure, showed U-shaped associations. Outdoor sunlight exposure duration showed positive, inverse, and nonlinear associations with a broad range of diseases. These findings highlight the potential importance of moderate exposure and appropriate sun protection but require validation in other populations.

papers.title: Health Information Literacy Moderates the Associations of Perceived Social Support with Insomnia and Infertility Psychological Distress in Women Undergoing Assisted Reproductive Technology: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Psychological distress is common among women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART). Perceived social support, insomnia, and health information literacy may be interrelated with psychological distress during fertility treatment, but their conditional relationships remain insufficiently understood. This study examined the indirect association between perceived social support and infertility psychological distress through insomnia and whether health information literacy moderated the associations among perceived social support, insomnia, and IPD. A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to August 2024, enrolling 1007 women undergoing ART at two tertiary hospitals in Wuhan, China. Standardized instruments, including the Perceived Social Support Scale (PSS), the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), the Everyday Health Information Literacy (HIL) questionnaire, and the Infertility Psychological Distress (IPD) Scale, were utilized for data collection. Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS Models 4 and 59 with 5000 bootstrap samples. Seven prespecified sociodemographic and clinical covariates were included in the analyses. PSS was negatively associated with IPD (B = -0.364, p < 0.001) and ISI (B = -0.094, p < 0.001). A significant indirect association between PSS and IPD through ISI was observed (indirect effect = -0.132, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.175, -0.094]). HIL significantly moderated the associations between PSS and ISI (B = -0.008, p < 0.001), between PSS and IPD (B = -0.029, p < 0.001), and between ISI and IPD (B = -0.071, p = 0.003). At higher levels of HIL, the negative associations of PSS with ISI and IPD were stronger, whereas the positive association between ISI and IPD was weaker. In this cross-sectional study, PSS was indirectly associated with IPD through ISI, and HIL modified the associations among PSS, ISI, and IPD. These findings suggest that social support, sleep problems, and HIL may be usefully considered together in psychosocial assessment during ART. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine the temporal and causal relationships among these factors.

papers.title: Avermectin poisoning with panic-like symptoms: a case series.
papers.abstract: High doses of avermectin, a macrolide derived from Streptomyces avermitilis, can cause coma, delirium, respiratory failure, hypotension, and acidosis. However, certain adverse toxicological effects and psychological implications remain unrecognized in patients undergoing parasuicide. Case 1: A 54-year-old man ingested approximately 500 mL avermectin benzylate. He was found to be somnolent 45 min later. Subsequently, the patient became unconscious with respiratory failure, hypotension, and acidosis (lactate, 16.2 mmol/L). Gastric lavage, mechanical ventilation, hemoperfusion, hemofiltration, and symptomatic treatments were administered. Three days after ingestion, the patient's primary symptoms were delirium and myoclonus, with a blood avermectin level of 110.06 μg/L. Thereafter, intermittent shaking, limb flexion, and muscle rigidity persisted. Thirteen days after ingestion, brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable. Electroencephalography revealed no epileptiform discharges. After psychiatric evaluation, the patient was assessed as having panic-like symptoms, and his symptoms improved significantly with specialized treatment. Case 2: A 33-year-old man was injected with approximately 5 mL of 1% avermectin in his left forearm. Two days later, he reported significant pain and swelling along with intermittent palpitations, dizziness, and limb tremors consistent with panic-like symptoms. His blood avermectin level was 0.02 μg/mL. After 7 days of treatment, the swelling subsided, and the panic-like symptoms resolved. Avermectin poisoning causes significant toxic effects, including respiratory failure, hypotension, acidosis, coma, and delirium. Intramuscular injections may result in localized swelling. Parasuicide patients may also present with panic-like symptoms requiring careful differential diagnosis.

papers.title: From driving (L0) to living (L5): Intergenerational car comfort concept by Etic-emic theory.
papers.abstract: This study explores intergenerational vehicle comfort using the Etic-Emic framework, translating a psychological concept into automotive guidelines. A scoping review identified 34 parameters, and trend analysis of 1789 Scopus articles (1953-2025) tracing comfort across vehicle generations. Expert interviews with 15 specialists classified them as Etic (relevant to L0 and L5) or Emic (emerging specifically in L5), suggesting additional factors. Group brainstorming refined classifications, yielding 44 parameters, including factors such as brand identity and cargo space. Safety, vibration control, and fuel efficiency were stable Etic parameters, whereas non-driving tasks, confidence to sleep or fully recline, legal liability transparency, and cybersecurity were Emic. The novel "Intergenerational Car Comfort" concept provides OEMs an actionable decision tool: its Etic-Emic matrix guides trade-offs, including safety constraints versus expectations to recline and sleep. Ultimately, it identifies legacy architectures to retain or those requiring new interior packaging and HMI solutions, providing a roadmap for next-generation automated vehicles.

papers.title: Effects of opioid-free intraoperative anesthesia versus opioid-based anesthesia on postoperative immune function in elderly patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty: a single-center, prospective, randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in elderly patients may involve postoperative immune suppression. This study compares intraoperative opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) and opioid-based anesthesia (OBA) effects on postoperative proportion of immune cells. The core pharmacological difference between groups lies in the intraoperative anesthetic regimen: the OBA group received sufentanil for induction and continuous remifentanil infusion for maintenance, while the OFA group replaced all intraoperative opioids with esketamine. Both groups received opioid-containing patient-controlled intravenous analgesia and rescue analgesia after surgery, and the opioid-free anesthesia protocol was only applied during the intraoperative phase. A single-center, prospective, randomized controlled trial of 60 patients (60-80 years) undergoing unilateral TKA. The opioid-free strategy was exclusively implemented during the intraoperative period, and both groups received identical opioid-inclusive postoperative analgesia. Patients were randomized into OFA (n = 30) and OBA (n = 30) groups. change in natural killer (NK) cell proportion. T-cell subsets (CD3⁺, CD4⁺, CD8⁺), B cells, dynamic/static visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) demands, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), hemodynamics, and adverse events. We conducted an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis in 60 patients (30 in each group). Baseline demographics and preoperative immune indices showed no significant differences between the groups. Compared with the levels one day before the operation, the postoperative reduction in NK cell proportion was significantly smaller in the OFA group than in the OBA group (Δ = -5.51% ± 4.89% vs. Δ = -10.12% ± 5.39%; P < 0.001). The OFA group demonstrated superior early postoperative analgesia, with lower dynamic and static VAS scores at 4-48 h (P < 0.05), reduced PCIA demands at 24 h (5.8 ± 0.9 vs. 7.2 ± 1.1) and 48 h (6.1 ± 1.0 vs. 8.5 ± 1.3; P < 0.05), and better PSQI (7.50 ± 3.34 vs. 10.86 ± 4.01; P < 0.001). The OFA group had significantly lower intraoperative vasoactive agent consumption (atropine, norepinephrine, ephedrine) and 72-hour postoperative opioid consumption (all P < 0.05), and exhibited superior postoperative functional exercise capacity (active knee flexion angle and maximum walking distance) at 48 and 72 h postoperatively (all P < 0.05). No significant differences were observed between the groups in CD8⁺ T cell, B cell proportions, extubation time, length of hospital stay, rescue analgesia rate or postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) incidence (all P > 0.05). In elderly patients undergoing unilateral total knee arthroplasty, intraoperative esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia was associated with a smaller decline in NK-cell proportion, superior early analgesia, and improved short-term sleep quality compared with opioid-based anesthesia.
